stem: A rectal suction biopsy is performed in a child with suspected Hirschsprung disease. Which result best supports the diagnosis?

options.text: Absence of ganglion cells in the bowel mucosa with a negative calretinin stain
Normal ganglion cells in the bowel mucosa with a positive calretinin stain
Absence of ganglion cells with a positive calretinin stain
Presence of ganglion cells with a negative calretinin stain
Normal ganglion cells in the bowel mucosa with a negative calretinin stain

explanation: Absence of ganglion cells with a negative calretinin stain supports Hirschsprung disease. This biopsy pattern indicates aganglionosis, which is the characteristic histological finding in the condition.

citations.source: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
citations.title: Additional Congenital Surgical Problems

rationale: The diagnosis of Hirschsprung disease is supported by aganglionosis on rectal suction biopsy, and calretinin staining is typically negative in affected bowel.

optionExplanations.A: Correct because the absence of ganglion cells and negative calretinin staining are the key biopsy findings that support Hirschsprung disease.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because normal ganglion cells and positive calretinin staining are not consistent with Hirschsprung disease.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because a positive calretinin stain does not support aganglionosis in Hirschsprung disease.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because the presence of ganglion cells argues against Hirschsprung disease.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because normal ganglion cells are not the diagnostic finding in Hirschsprung disease, even if calretinin is negative.
